title: The Most Important Question in Teaching
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Dave Stuart Jr. argues that teachers burn out largely because they are perpetually reacting to the latest lesson or meeting instead of asking what matters most. Working conditions seem designed to produce near-crazed, nonstop teachers, and the desire to be great, poorly understood, demands an inhuman amount of effort. He draws on Dan Pink's line that greatness and nearsightedness are incompatible and describes his own response: reading the professional literature, feeling overwhelmed by competing lists of must-dos, and insisting on one question, what is it for? He applies the question to English instruction and to the whole school day, noting that students find school disorienting when each class offers a different idea of its purpose. The post ends by promising his answer elsewhere.
points: Teacher attrition is partly a thinking problem: without a clear view of what matters most, greatness seems to require unlimited effort.
Pink's 'greatness and nearsightedness are incompatible' frames the need to lift one's sights toward a coherent purpose.
Competing professional prescriptions add up to an impossible workload unless a single organizing question is asked.
Students' apathy may partly stem from school not making sense when each class and grade offers a different take on purpose.
quotes: After all, it’s almost like the working conditions of today’s teacher were carefully designed to create this kind of near-crazed person, perpetually reacting, rarely thinking deeply, caught in a nonstop cycle of wake up, work like a maniac, crash into bed, repeat nine months a year.

But then once you get into the work a bit, you realize that it takes this inhuman amount of effort to do everything you think greatness requires. This is because, frankly, you’re not thinking clearly enough about greatness — you have a very poor understanding of it and of the work you’re doing.
Greatness and nearsightedness are incompatible. Meaningful achievement depends on lifting one’s sights and pushing toward the horizon.

I quickly internalized a feeling that every secondary English teacher knows well — this sense that you’re doing a bad job and a disservice to kids if you’re not completing a list of things that adds up to about 120 hours of work per week.
I started sensing that one root of my students’ apathy lay in the simple reality that school didn’t make sense. My students wanted to succeed in life. I think all kids want to do well.
What was the fundamental fact of education, the starting point from which you might be able to build a coherent sense of the whole, and thereby streamline the work and make it sustainable?
